title: IssueFlow product vision, goals, and v1 non-goals
questions: What is IssueFlow?
Who is IssueFlow for?
What is explicitly out of scope for version 1?
Does IssueFlow v1 integrate with GitHub, Slack, or Jira?
text:
IssueFlow v1.0 is a multi-user, self-hosted web application for small and medium-sized teams. Teams use it to create projects, manage issues, track progress, collaborate, and organize work. The tagline is "Your work. Your issues. Your control." The default appearance is a dark theme. Deployment is local, through Docker Compose.

The product is manual-first. A person creates each issue, assigns people, selects priority, updates status, adds tags, creates subtasks, and marks work complete. The system may generate issue IDs, record activity, calculate dashboard statistics, persist data, and send reminders from dates a person entered. It does not independently make project-management decisions.

Product goals:

1. Provide a premium, minimalist user interface.
2. Make issue creation and management fast and intuitive.
3. Support multiple team members with role-based permissions.
4. Provide essential project-management and collaboration functionality.
5. Keep application data on the user's own infrastructure.
6. Make installation and operation simple through Docker.
7. Avoid unnecessary automation and feature complexity.

Version 1 non-goals are: AI-generated issues or descriptions; automatic issue assignment; automatic status changes; automatic issue creation; GitHub or GitLab integrations; Slack integrations; external Jira synchronization; sprint planning and velocity tracking; time tracking and billing; public issue portals; complex workflow automation; email automation.

The intended product outcome is that a team can run its issue-tracking workflow in IssueFlow and keep full control of its data and decisions. The PRD directs a polished, practical issue tracker with a short feature set. Build priority is excellent UI, simple workflows, manual control, reliable issues/comments/attachments/activity, easy Docker deployment, and a maintainable codebase.

title: Manual actions versus allowed automatic behavior
questions: What may IssueFlow change automatically?
Can a background job change issue status, assignee, or priority?
Are due-date reminders allowed to edit the issue?
Does completing every subtask mark the parent Done?
text:
IssueFlow principles are manual-first, minimalist, consistent, fast, secure, self-hosted, reliable, and transparent. Transparent means the system records who changed what and when. Reliable means data survives container restarts. Secure means every operation checks permissions.

People perform these actions themselves: create issue, assign issue, change status, set priority, add tags, set due date, add comments, create subtasks, add dependencies, upload attachments, complete issue, and delete issue. Delete requires confirmation.

The system may do only these things on its own: generate the issue ID, record timestamps, record activity, calculate statistics, send due-date reminders from user-entered dates, and persist data.

No background process may autonomously change an issue's status, assignee, priority, or any other business field. Dragging a Kanban card is a user action. The board must not move cards by itself. Parent completion statistics are calculated automatically, and the parent issue is never automatically marked Done. Dependencies never change issue status. Dashboard values are calculated from existing records and must not create or modify issues. Due-date reminders use dates people entered, and notifications must not change the underlying issue.

Activity entries are produced by the server. The client must not be trusted to supply the activity record.

title: Application roles and the permissions the PRD states
questions: What roles does IssueFlow have?
What can an Admin, Manager, and Member do?
Does a Member create projects?
Where is project membership separate from application role?
text:
IssueFlow has three application roles.

Admin has full application access, user management, project management, and settings.

Manager can create projects, manage issues, assign members, and manage tags and workflows.

Member can view permitted projects, create and update permitted issues, comment, and upload attachments.

"Permitted" is project scope. Project membership is a separate relationship from the application role. The PRD requires role-based access control on every protected operation, plus project-level authorization. Every issue, project, attachment, comment, and notification access is checked against the authenticated user's permissions.

The role table does not give Member permission to create projects, manage users, assign project members, or manage tags. Admin is the role that manages users and settings. Manager is the role that creates projects and assigns members.

The phrase "manage workflows" appears in the Manager role. Version 1 also lists complex workflow automation as a non-goal, and it defines one fixed status set. The PRD does not describe a workflow designer.

Bulk actions apply only to issues the user explicitly selects and is authorized to modify. Exports must respect project permissions. The PRD says export requires appropriate permissions and does not name the role. Deleting an issue requires confirmation; the PRD does not name which role may delete.

title: Authentication, sessions, and account administration
questions: How do users sign in to IssueFlow?
Can people register themselves?
Who creates accounts?
What happens when a user is deactivated?
How is the first admin created?
text:
IssueFlow uses email and password authentication, secure password hashing, and session-based authentication. The chosen library is Better Auth. Authentication entities are User, Account, Session, and Verification, and they must follow the Better Auth adapter schema actually in use.

There is no public registration. An admin creates accounts. An admin can deactivate or reactivate users. Inactive users cannot log in. Users can change their own passwords. Deactivated users must not lose historical activity records.

Cookies that carry the session are HTTP-only and use appropriate security settings. Login is rate limited. Credentials must not be hardcoded. A secure initial admin account is created through a documented bootstrap process.

Sign-in, sign-out, and session endpoints are managed by Better Auth. The PRD does not specify password complexity, session lifetime, multi-factor authentication, email verification behavior, or the invite and temporary-password flow. The Verification entity exists because the Better Auth adapter schema includes it.

title: Overview dashboard contents and calculation rules
questions: What does the IssueFlow dashboard show?
Can the dashboard create or edit issues?
How fast should the dashboard load?
text:
The dashboard is a concise overview of project activity and assigned work. The Overview screen is P0. Dashboard values are calculated from existing records. The dashboard must not create or modify issues.

Required values and lists:

- Total active issues.
- Issues assigned to the current user.
- Issues in progress.
- Blocked issues.
- Completed issues.
- Upcoming deadlines.
- Recently updated issues.
- My assigned issues.
- Quick access to projects.
- Notifications and reminders.

The initial performance target is dashboard loading under 2 seconds under normal test conditions, for an initial scale of 10 to 20 concurrent users and 50,000 or more issues. These targets are validation goals, not guaranteed limits. The roadmap places dashboard and reminders in phase 10, priority P1, while the Overview screen itself is P0. The acceptance scenario requires the dashboard to reflect updated issue data before the MVP is functionally complete.

title: Projects, project keys, members, and tags
questions: What fields does a project have?
Can a project key change after issues exist?
What project actions exist?
Are tags global or per project?
text:
Users with the right permissions can create and manage projects. Project screens and project details are P0.

Project fields are: project name (human-readable), project key (unique short identifier such as ECOM), description (optional), members (users on the project), tags (project-specific), status (active or archived), created by, and created at.

Project actions are: create and edit projects, archive projects, view the project overview, add and remove members, view project issues and the board, manage project tags, and view project activity.

Project keys must be unique. Once issues exist, changing a project key requires a safe migration mechanism. Without that mechanism, the key is immutable. The PRD does not specify the migration steps, whether existing issue keys are rewritten, or whether project restore exists after archive.

Tags are created and managed manually. Tags belong to one project. A tag has a custom name and a selectable color. An issue can have multiple tags. Users can search and filter by tag, rename a tag, and delete a tag with appropriate handling of linked issues. The PRD does not define whether delete removes links only or blocks delete while links exist.

title: Issue fields, types, statuses, and priorities
questions: What fields does an issue have?
Which issue fields are required?
What are the issue types, statuses, and priorities?
Who is the reporter?
text:
Issue management is the central module. Every action that changes issue data is explicitly initiated by a user.

Issue fields:

| Field | Type | Required |
|---|---|---|
| Issue title | Text | Yes |
| Description | Markdown | No |
| Project | Project reference | Yes |
| Issue key | Generated ID | Automatic |
| Issue type | Enum | Yes |
| Status | Enum | Yes |
| Priority | Enum | Yes |
| Assignee | User reference | No |
| Reporter | User reference | Automatic |
| Tags | Multiple references | No |
| Due date | Date | No |
| Parent issue | Issue reference | No |
| Created at | Timestamp | Automatic |
| Updated at | Timestamp | Automatic |

Issue types are Bug, Task, Story, Feature, and Research.

Default statuses are Backlog, To Do, In Progress, In Review, Blocked, and Done.

Priorities are Critical, High, Medium, and Low.

The reporter is set automatically. The PRD does not say the reporter can be edited. Assignee, tags, due date, description, and parent issue are optional. An issue references one project.

The field table does not include an archived flag, a deleted flag, or a board rank. Archive, restore, delete, and persisted card order are required behaviors elsewhere in the PRD, so the physical columns for those behaviors are an implementation detail the PRD leaves open.

title: Issue key format and concurrent unique numbering
questions: What does an issue key look like?
How are issue numbers generated when two users create issues at once?
Are issue keys unique?
text:
An issue key combines the project key with a generated number. Examples in the PRD are ECOM-001, ECOM-002, ECOM-003, WEB-001, and WEB-002. The number is per project. Issue keys must be unique.

Issue numbers are generated inside a database transaction and stay unique when multiple users create issues at the same time. Issue IDs use the same transactional rule. Database rule 1 says issue IDs are generated safely inside transactions. Database rule 2 says issue keys are unique.

The examples use three digits. The PRD does not state the width after 999, whether numbers may be skipped, or whether a rolled-back create may reuse a number. Changing a project key after issues exist requires a safe migration; otherwise the project key is immutable, which also freezes the prefix of existing issue keys.

title: Issue actions, archive, restore, delete, and duplicate
questions: What actions can a user take on an issue?
Is delete the same as archive?
What does duplicating an issue mean?
Which bulk actions exist?
text:
Issue actions, each started by a person, are: create and edit an issue; change status and priority; assign a member; add or remove tags; set or update a due date; create subtasks; add dependencies; add comments; upload attachments; duplicate an issue; archive or restore an issue; delete an issue with confirmation.

Archive and delete are both required. Restore applies to an archived issue. The PRD does not define whether delete is a hard delete, whether activity and attachments are removed with the issue, or whether a project can be restored after archive.

"Duplicate an issue" is an action that creates another issue. "Duplicates" is also a dependency relationship type. The PRD does not say which fields the duplicate action copies, and it does not say that the action creates a Duplicates link.

The All Issues page requires explicit selection for bulk actions. Bulk actions apply only to issues the user selects and is authorized to modify. The PRD does not list the bulk operations.

title: All Issues, My Issues, search, sort, and saved filters
questions: How do users find issues?
Which fields can be searched, filtered, and sorted?
What saved filters are listed as examples?
Are saved filters shared?
text:
All Issues is the primary discovery screen and is P0. My Issues is also P0. Saved Filters as a screen is P1. Search and filters are roadmap phase 5, priority P0.

The All Issues page shows issues in a clean, configurable table. Users search by issue key and title. Users filter by project, status, priority, assignee, tags, and due date. Users sort by creation date, update date, priority, and due date. The page has pagination, configurable visible columns, saved filters, and explicit selection for bulk actions.

Search supports issue key and title. The same filter fields apply. Users can save frequently used filter combinations. Example saved filters are My Open Issues, Critical Bugs, Blocked Issues, Overdue Issues, and Issues Due This Week.

The initial target for a typical issue search is under 1 second under normal test conditions, at a data target of 50,000 or more issues.

The PRD does not say whether saved filters belong to one user or are shared, what JSON shape a filter uses, or whether column configuration is stored per user. It does not require full-text search of descriptions or comments. Search is key and title.

title: Kanban board columns, drag-and-drop, and card order
questions: What columns does the Kanban board have?
What does dragging a card do?
What does a card show?
Does the board reorder cards by itself?
text:
The Kanban board displays issues organized by status. The Board screen is P0. Roadmap phase 6 is the Kanban board, priority P0. Drag-and-drop uses dnd-kit.

Default columns, in order, are Backlog, To Do, In Progress, In Review, Blocked, and Done. These names match the default statuses.

Requirements: drag-and-drop issue cards; status changes that a person initiates; cards show title, issue key, priority, assignee, and tags; filter by project, assignee, priority, and tags; open issue details by selecting a card; persist card ordering; give clear feedback after a successful status update.

Dragging a card is a user action. The application must not move cards automatically. On smaller screens the board supports horizontal scrolling.

The PRD does not say whether card order is shared by the project or private to the user, how concurrent drags are resolved, or whether columns can be renamed or hidden in v1.

title: Issue detail layout and editable properties
questions: What does the issue detail page show?
Which properties are editable?
How does issue detail behave on mobile?
How fast should issue detail load?
text:
The issue detail view uses a clean two-column layout. Issue Details is a P0 screen. Create Issue is also P0. The initial target is issue detail loading under 1 second under normal test conditions.

Main content contains the issue title, Markdown description, subtasks, dependencies, attachments, comments, and activity history.

The properties panel contains status, priority, assignee, reporter, project, tags, due date, and issue type.

All properties are editable through clear, direct interactions, subject to permissions. On mobile, issue detail panels stack vertically.

The properties panel lists project as editable. The PRD does not specify a move-between-projects operation, what happens to the issue key if the project changes, or whether project-specific tags survive that move.

title: Subtasks, their own keys, and parent completion statistics
questions: How do subtasks work?
Does a subtask get its own issue key?
Does finishing all subtasks complete the parent?
What is the subtasks API?
text:
Users manually create subtasks under a parent issue. The parent is stored as the parent issue reference on the child. Each subtask receives its own issue key. Subtasks have their own status, priority, assignee, and due date. Users can edit and delete subtasks. The parent issue displays subtask completion statistics.

Example from the PRD:

```text
ECOM-101  Implement checkout
  ECOM-102  Create checkout UI
  ECOM-103  Integrate payment API
  ECOM-104  Add payment validation
```

Parent completion statistics are calculated automatically. The parent issue is never automatically marked Done.

The API group for subtasks is `/issues/:id/subtasks` under the `/api/v1` prefix. Roadmap phase 8 covers subtasks and dependencies at priority P0.

The PRD does not set a nesting depth limit, and it does not say whether subtasks appear as normal rows on All Issues and on the Kanban board.

title: Issue dependency types and blocking rules
questions: What issue relationship types exist?
Are Blocks and Is blocked by stored separately?
What dependency links are rejected?
Does a blocking link change status to Blocked?
text:
Users manually link related issues. Supported relationship types are Blocks, Is blocked by, Relates to, and Duplicates. The PRD says Is blocked by is the inverse representation of Blocks.

Requirements: search for existing issues; select a related issue and a relationship type; view linked issues in issue details; remove dependencies; prevent self-dependencies; prevent circular blocking relationships.

The system must not automatically change issue status because of dependencies. A Blocks link does not set status to Blocked. Blocked remains a status a person selects.

Database rule 4: circular blocking dependencies must be rejected. The PRD does not say whether cycle detection is only direct (A blocks B and B blocks A) or transitive (A blocks B blocks C blocks A). It does not say whether Relates to or Duplicates are symmetric, and it does not apply the circularity rule to those types.

The API group is `/issues/:id/dependencies`. The Dependency entity stores issue relationships. Project and issue relationships must be validated.

title: Comments, mentions, and server-written activity history
questions: What comment actions exist?
Which changes are written to activity history?
What does an activity record contain?
Can the client submit an activity record?
text:
Comments support add, edit own comments subject to permissions, and delete own comments subject to permissions. The UI shows author and timestamp. Comments support Markdown.

Activity history records these events: issue created; issue title or description changed; status changed; priority changed; assignee changed; tags changed; due date changed; comment added; attachment uploaded; dependency added or removed; issue archived or restored.

Each activity record includes the actor, the action, the previous value when applicable, the new value when applicable, and a timestamp. The server generates activity entries. They are not trusted from the client. Database rule 5: activity records are written in the same transaction as the relevant issue update. Database rule 6: deactivated users must not lose historical activity records.

The API groups are `/issues/:id/comments` and `/issues/:id/activity`. The entities are Comment and ActivityLog.

The activity list does not include issue deleted, issue duplicated, subtask added, or comment edited. The PRD does not say whether editing or deleting a comment writes activity. Mentions are optional: a notification type exists only if mentions are implemented.

title: Markdown in descriptions and comments, and sanitization
questions: Which Markdown features are supported?
Why must Markdown be sanitized?
Which editor is specified?
text:
Descriptions and comments support headings, bold and italic, strikethrough, bulleted and numbered lists, checklists, links, inline code, code blocks, and blockquotes.

Markdown is sanitized before rendering so script injection and unsafe HTML cannot run. This is a security requirement, together with Zod input validation.

The Markdown editor is TipTap. Roadmap phase 7 is comments, activity, and Markdown, priority P0.

The PRD does not say whether checklist checkboxes are interactive. If a person toggles a checkbox inside the description, that is an edit of issue data and must be a user-initiated save. The spec does not define a separate checklist entity.

title: Attachment types, limits, storage, and authorized download
questions: Which file types can be uploaded?
What is the maximum attachment size?
Where are files stored?
Can attachment URLs be public?
text:
Users can upload files to issues. Attachments are roadmap phase 9, priority P1. The acceptance scenario and the definition of done both require secure attachments before the MVP is complete.

Initial supported formats are PNG, JPG and JPEG, WEBP, PDF, TXT, CSV, DOCX, XLSX, and ZIP. The default maximum file size is 20 MB.

The product shows file name, size, and uploader. Users can download attachments and delete them after a permission check. Files are stored on a persistent Docker volume named `attachments`. Attachment metadata is stored in PostgreSQL on the Attachment entity. Files are served through authenticated, authorized endpoints. The server validates MIME type, extension, and file size.

Attachments must survive container restarts and application upgrades. There are no public attachment URLs. A database backup without the matching attachment files is not a complete backup. Database rule 8: files live outside the database, metadata lives in PostgreSQL. Database rule 9: database and attachment backups are coordinated.

The PRD does not specify the on-disk path layout, virus scanning, ZIP content inspection, or what happens to the file if the database transaction fails.

title: In-app notifications and due-date reminders
questions: Which notification types exist?
Are reminders sent by email?
What process sends due-date reminders?
Can a reminder change the issue?
text:
MVP notifications are in-app only. Email automation is a v1 non-goal. The Notifications screen is P1. Dashboard and reminders are roadmap phase 10, priority P1. The acceptance scenario requires due-date reminders to appear when appropriate.

Notification types are: issue assigned; comment added; user mentioned, if mentions are implemented; due tomorrow; due today; overdue issue.

The product provides a notification center, an unread count, mark one notification as read, and mark all as read. A periodic background job checks reminders. The job must prevent duplicate reminders for the same event and user. The worker is a separate container using the same application code and the same PostgreSQL database. Background jobs use pg-boss.

Due-date reminders use dates people entered. Notifications must not change the underlying issue. The Notification entity stores user notifications. The API group is `/notifications`.

The PRD does not define the recipient of a comment notification, the timezone that decides "tomorrow" and "today", the check interval, or whether a changed due date creates a new reminder after one was already sent. Status changes, priority changes, and dependency changes are not notification types.

title: CSV and JSON export, backups, and restore
questions: What can users export, and in which formats?
What must a backup include?
How many backup sets are kept?
When is restore tested?
text:
Users with appropriate permissions can export all permitted issues, filtered issues, project issues, and individual issue data. Formats are CSV and JSON. Exports respect project permissions and the applied filters. Endpoints are `/exports/issues.csv` and `/exports/issues.json` under `/api/v1`. Export and backup/restore are roadmap phase 11, priority P1. The acceptance scenario requires export of permitted issue data.

Backup requirements: a PostgreSQL database backup; an attachment directory backup; a daily automated backup capability; seven daily backup sets by default; backups may be stored outside Docker volumes; restoration steps are documented; restoration is tested before the product is declared production-ready.

A database backup without its corresponding attachments is not a complete backup. The definition of done requires backup and restore procedures to be documented and tested. The PRD does not choose the dump tool, the schedule clock, or whether restore returns pg-boss jobs.

title: Visual design, navigation, screens, and responsive behavior
questions: What should IssueFlow look like?
What is in the sidebar and top bar?
Which screens are P0 and which are P1?
How does the layout behave on a phone?
text:
The visual direction is minimalist dark SaaS. The default appearance is a dark theme. It should feel like a modern professional productivity application. Styling is Tailwind CSS. Components are shadcn/ui. Icons are Lucide. Typography is Inter.

Visual characteristics: deep charcoal background; a slightly lighter sidebar; dark gray surfaces; subtle borders; indigo primary accent; green success; amber warning; red critical; 8 to 12 px border radii; minimal icons; consistent spacing; a clear type hierarchy; subtle hover and focus states.

The design avoids excessive gradients, bright colors everywhere, too many dashboard cards, heavy borders, unnecessary animations, cluttered navigation, and overloaded issue forms.

Sidebar order: Overview, All Issues, My Issues, Board, Projects, Tags, Team, Settings.

Top navigation: current page title, search, notifications, user profile, and a primary action such as Create Issue.

P0 screens, required for the first usable MVP: Login, Overview dashboard, All Issues, Create Issue, Issue Details, Projects, Project Details, Kanban Board, My Issues, Team Management.

P1 screens, which complete the planned MVP experience: Notifications, Settings, Saved Filters.

The experience is desktop-first. It supports tablet layouts and mobile browsing with basic issue operations. The sidebar collapses on smaller screens. Tables adapt to smaller widths. Issue detail panels stack vertically on mobile. Kanban scrolls horizontally.

The PRD does not require a light theme, localization, or a keyboard alternative for drag-and-drop. Settings contents are not listed.

title: Modular monolith, technology stack, and process split
questions: What architecture does IssueFlow use?
What is the technology stack?
Which process runs reminders?
Where does business logic live?
text:
IssueFlow is a modular monolith. It is one deployable application, not a set of microservices. The main parts are a browser UI, a Next.js application that contains both the UI and the REST API, PostgreSQL, a separate worker process that uses the same application code and the same database, and persistent file storage for attachments.

Stack:

| Layer | Technology |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Next.js and TypeScript |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS |
| UI components | shadcn/ui |
| Icons | Lucide |
| Backend | Next.js Route Handlers |
| API validation | Zod |
| Forms | React Hook Form |
| Authentication | Better Auth |
| ORM | Prisma |
| Database | PostgreSQL 17 |
| Kanban drag-and-drop | dnd-kit |
| Markdown editor | TipTap |
| Background jobs | pg-boss |
| File storage | Docker persistent volume |
| Unit testing | Vitest |
| E2E testing | Playwright |
| Containerization | Docker and Docker Compose |

Use compatible stable package versions, pin them in the lockfile, and keep the database, ORM, authentication adapter, and framework versions consistent.

Route handlers validate input, authenticate the user, check permissions, and call a service layer. Business logic is not implemented inside route handlers. The worker shares that service code so reminder behavior cannot drift from the web process. The worker still must not change business fields.

title: Docker Compose services, volumes, bootstrap, and install path
questions: How is IssueFlow installed?
Which containers are required?
Which data survives a restart?
Is PostgreSQL published on the host?
text:
Users install IssueFlow with Docker Desktop or Docker Engine plus Docker Compose. They do not install Node.js, npm, or PostgreSQL on the host. The definition of done requires that Docker installation works without host Node.js or PostgreSQL, and that migrations work on a fresh database and on an existing one.

Install:

```bash
git clone <repository-url>
cd issueflow
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up --build
```

Startup order: start PostgreSQL; wait for database health; run database migrations; initialize required application data; start the application; start the background worker.

Containers:

| Container | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| app | Main web application |
| db | PostgreSQL database |
| migrate | Database migrations and bootstrap |
| worker | Reminder processing |

Persistent volumes are `postgres_data` and `attachments`. The database is not publicly exposed by default. The application is at `http://localhost:3000`.

A secure initial admin is created by a documented bootstrap process. Default production credentials are not hardcoded. For LAN access, operators may publish the application port and restrict it with a firewall. Public internet deployment requires HTTPS and additional security configuration.

Roadmap phase 1 is Docker, database, migrations, and the app foundation, priority P0. The acceptance scenario starts with an admin bringing the stack up with Docker Compose and ends with a container restart that keeps application data.

title: Database entities and transactional integrity rules
questions: Which database entities does IssueFlow v1 include?
Which writes must share a transaction?
What integrity rules does the database enforce?
text:
The initial database model includes these entities:

| Entity | Purpose |
|---|---|
| User | User accounts and roles |
| Account | Authentication provider credentials |
| Session | Authentication sessions |
| Verification | Authentication verification tokens |
| Project | Project information |
| ProjectMember | Project membership |
| Issue | Main issue records |
| Tag | Project tags |
| IssueTag | Issue and tag relationship |
| Comment | Issue comments |
| ActivityLog | Issue history |
| Attachment | File metadata |
| Dependency | Issue relationships |
| Notification | User notifications |
| SavedFilter | Saved search filters |

User, Account, Session, and Verification follow the Better Auth adapter schema. Role is an application field on the user and must fit that schema.

Database rules:

1. Issue IDs are generated safely inside transactions.
2. Issue keys are unique.
3. Project and issue relationships are validated.
4. Circular blocking dependencies are rejected.
5. Activity records are written in the same transaction as the relevant issue update.
6. Deactivated users do not lose historical activity records.
7. Common filters have suitable database indexes.
8. Attachment bytes are stored outside the database. Metadata is in PostgreSQL.
9. Database backups and attachment backups are coordinated.

Common filters from the product are project, status, priority, assignee, tags, and due date, plus search by issue key and title, and sort by created, updated, priority, and due date. The PRD requires indexes for those filters and does not name the index list.

title: REST API envelope, prefix, and endpoint groups
questions: What is the IssueFlow API prefix and response shape?
Which endpoint groups exist?
What must every endpoint do before business logic?
What is the typical API latency target?
text:
All application APIs use the prefix `/api/v1`.

Success:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {},
  "message": "Operation completed successfully"
}
```

Error:

```json
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Invalid request"
  }
}
```

The example error code is `VALIDATION_ERROR`. The PRD does not publish a full error-code catalog, a pagination shape, or idempotency rules.

Endpoint groups:

| Module | Examples |
|---|---|
| Authentication | Better Auth sign-in, sign-out, and session endpoints |
| Users | `GET/POST /users`, `PATCH /users/:id` |
| Projects | `GET/POST /projects`, `PATCH /projects/:id` |
| Project members | `/projects/:id/members` |
| Issues | `GET/POST /issues`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /issues/:id` |
| Subtasks | `/issues/:id/subtasks` |
| Tags | `/projects/:id/tags`, `/tags/:id` |
| Comments | `/issues/:id/comments` |
| Attachments | `/issues/:id/attachments` |
| Dependencies | `/issues/:id/dependencies` |
| Activity | `/issues/:id/activity` |
| Notifications | `/notifications` |
| Saved filters | `/filters` |
| Exports | `/exports/issues.csv`, `/exports/issues.json` |

Every endpoint validates input, authenticates the user, checks permissions, and calls the service layer. Business logic stays out of route handlers. Validation uses Zod.

The initial target for a typical API response is under 500 ms, excluding file transfers. Export and attachment download are file transfers. Browser support for the UI is current Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari.

Better Auth manages its own sign-in, sign-out, and session endpoints. The PRD does not say those routes use this JSON envelope.

title: Security controls required even for local installs
questions: What security controls does IssueFlow require?
Are local installs exempt from authorization?
Who can download an attachment?
Which admin actions are audited?
text:
Security applies to local self-hosted installations. A local deployment does not drop these controls.

Required controls: secure password hashing; HTTP-only authentication cookies with appropriate security settings; role-based access control; project-level authorization; Zod input validation; file upload validation; Markdown sanitization before render; protection against SQL injection; login rate limiting; secure secret management; audit logging for important administrative actions; no public attachment URLs; no hardcoded credentials; no database port exposure by default.

Every issue, project, attachment, comment, and notification access is checked against the authenticated user's permissions. Prisma is the ORM, which is the specified way queries are constructed. Attachment endpoints are authenticated and authorized. MIME type, extension, and file size are validated. The default size cap is 20 MB.

The PRD requires audit logging for important administrative actions and does not list those actions. It requires login rate limiting and does not state a general API rate limit. It requires HTTPS when the application is exposed to the public internet.

title: Performance targets, acceptance scenario, roadmap, and definition of done
questions: When is the IssueFlow MVP functionally complete?
What are the performance targets?
What is the difference between P0 and P1?
What is the build order?
text:
Initial performance targets, to be validated on representative hardware and data, are: dashboard load under 2 seconds; issue detail load under 1 second; typical issue search under 1 second; typical API response under 500 ms excluding file transfers; 10 to 20 concurrent users; 50,000 or more issues; 20 MB default attachment size; data kept across container restarts; current Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari.

P0 screens are essential for the first usable MVP. P1 screens complete the planned MVP experience. P1 on the roadmap is sequence, and the completion bar still includes that work.

The MVP is functionally complete when this scenario succeeds:

1. An admin starts IssueFlow with Docker Compose.
2. The admin logs in.
3. The admin creates a project.
4. The admin creates team members.
5. The admin adds members to the project.
6. A member manually creates an issue.
7. The application generates a unique issue key.
8. The member sets status, priority, assignee, tags, and due date.
9. The member creates subtasks.
10. The member adds issue dependencies.
11. The member adds a Markdown comment.
12. The member uploads an attachment.
13. The member manually moves the issue across Kanban columns.
14. The activity history records the changes.
15. The dashboard reflects the updated issue data.
16. Due-date reminders appear when appropriate.
17. The member exports permitted issue data.
18. The containers restart without losing application data.

Tests also verify that unauthorized users cannot access or modify restricted resources.

Roadmap phases: (1) Docker, database, migrations, app foundation, P0. (2) Authentication, users, roles, permissions, P0. (3) Projects and membership, P0. (4) Issue CRUD and issue details, P0. (5) Search, filters, tags, saved filters, P0. (6) Kanban, P0. (7) Comments, activity, Markdown, P0. (8) Subtasks and dependencies, P0. (9) Attachments, P1. (10) Dashboard and reminders, P1. (11) Export and backup/restore, P1. (12) Testing, security review, and production packaging, P0.

The MVP is done when core features work end to end; the UI matches the dark design; every work-management change is user-initiated; role and project permissions are enforced; important issue changes are recorded; attachments are securely stored; data persists across restarts; Docker install needs no host Node.js or PostgreSQL; migrations work on fresh and existing databases; automated tests cover critical workflows; backup and restore are documented and tested.

Vitest covers unit tests. Playwright covers end-to-end tests. The PRD does not set a coverage percentage.

title: Decisions the PRD leaves open
questions: What does the IssueFlow PRD leave unspecified?
Who can delete an issue?
Are saved filters private?
What timezone do due reminders use?
Can issues be nested more than one level?
text:
These items are absent from IssueFlow PRD v1.0. An answer grounded in this corpus says they are unspecified. It does not pick a behavior and call it a requirement.

GAP-01 Permission matrix. The role table names Admin, Manager, and Member capabilities. It does not map each action to a role. Unspecified actions include delete issue, archive project, export, change settings, edit another person's comment, and whether Admin can see a project without a ProjectMember row.

GAP-02 Workflows. Manager may "manage workflows." Complex workflow automation is a non-goal, and statuses are one fixed enum. No workflow designer is specified.

GAP-03 Archive and delete persistence. Issues can be archived, restored, and deleted with confirmation. Projects can be archived. The issue field list has no archived or deleted column. Cascade behavior for comments, attachments, subtasks, dependencies, and activity is unspecified. Project restore is unspecified.

GAP-04 Duplicate action. Duplicate issue is an action. Duplicates is also a link type. The copied field set is unspecified. Creating a Duplicates link as part of the action is unspecified.

GAP-05 Bulk actions. Selection and authorization are required. The operation list is unspecified.

GAP-06 Saved filters and columns. Ownership, sharing, and the stored filter shape are unspecified. Column configuration persistence is unspecified.

GAP-07 Kanban rank. Card order is persisted. Shared versus per-user order, and concurrent drag behavior, are unspecified. Custom columns are unspecified.

GAP-08 Issue keys after 999. Examples use three digits. Width, skipped numbers, and reuse after a rolled-back insert are unspecified. Project-key migration steps are unspecified.

GAP-09 Subtasks. Nesting depth is unspecified. Visibility of subtasks on All Issues and Kanban is unspecified.

GAP-10 Dependencies. Transitive cycle detection is unspecified. Symmetry of Relates to and Duplicates is unspecified. Only blocking cycles are mentioned.

GAP-11 Moving an issue. The detail panel lists project as editable. Moving projects, rewriting the issue key, and keeping project tags are unspecified.

GAP-12 Activity coverage. Recorded events are listed. Delete, duplicate, comment edit, and comment delete are not in that list.

GAP-13 Mentions. The mention notification exists only if mentions are implemented. Mention syntax and recipients are unspecified.

GAP-14 Reminder timing. Timezone, schedule, and behavior after a due date change are unspecified. Comment notification recipients are unspecified. Status and priority changes are not notification types.

GAP-15 Accounts. Password policy, session lifetime, multi-factor authentication, and the admin invite flow are unspecified. Bootstrap is "documented" and the mechanism is unspecified.

GAP-16 API details. Pagination, the error-code catalog beyond VALIDATION_ERROR, and whether Better Auth routes use the JSON envelope are unspecified.

GAP-17 Concurrency. updatedAt exists. Optimistic locking and lost-update behavior are unspecified.

GAP-18 Files. On-disk layout, orphan files, malware scanning, and ZIP contents are unspecified.

GAP-19 Audit. Important administrative actions are audited. The event list is unspecified.

GAP-20 Settings. The Settings screen is P1. Its contents are unspecified. Light theme, localization, and a keyboard path for drag-and-drop are not required by the PRD.

GAP-21 Search technology. Search is issue key and title. Description and comment search are not required. The index type is unspecified aside from "suitable indexes."

title: Advisory defaults for the open PRD decisions
questions: What implementation defaults are proposed for IssueFlow gaps?
Are these defaults part of the PRD?
How should blocking links be stored?
text:
These defaults are proposals for the gaps in `issueflow.prd.v1.gaps`. They are not requirements of IssueFlow PRD v1.0. A RAG answer labels them as proposals.

R-01 Authorization. Check application role and project membership on every protected operation. Admin has application-wide access. Manager and Member act only inside projects where they have a ProjectMember row. Member can create and update issues, comment, and upload in those projects. Manager adds and removes members and manages tags. Only Admin creates, deactivates, and reactivates users and opens Settings.

R-02 Workflows. Ship the fixed status enum only. Do not build a workflow designer in v1. Treat "manage workflows" as managing work inside that fixed set.

R-03 Archive. Store `archivedAt` on issues and projects. Archive hides records from active views and is reversible. Delete is a separate confirmed action. Keep activity rows for deactivated users. Decide cascade before coding delete, and do not invent a cascade in the meantime.

R-04 Duplicate action. Copy title, description, type, priority, tags, project, and due date into a new issue. Leave assignee empty. Do not copy comments, attachments, activity, or subtasks. Do not create a Duplicates link unless the user adds one.

R-05 Bulk actions. Allow status, assignee, add tag, remove tag, and archive on the explicit selection. Require the same permission as the single-issue action. Leave bulk delete out until GAP-03 is decided.

R-06 Saved filters. Store them per user. The SavedFilter row holds the user, a name, and the filter JSON for project, status, priority, assignee, tags, and due date.

R-07 Kanban. Store one shared fractional rank per issue inside its status, scoped to the project. A drag writes status and rank in one transaction and writes activity for a status change. Reject the write if `updatedAt` does not match.

R-08 Keys. Keep a per-project counter updated in the same transaction as the insert. Never reuse a value. Render at least three digits and allow the decimal width to grow, so the key after ECOM-999 is ECOM-1000.

R-09 Subtasks. Allow one parent level in v1. Show subtasks on All Issues and Kanban because they are issues with their own keys and statuses. The parent completion fraction is a count of children in Done over all children.

R-10 Dependencies. Store one directed row for Blocks. Render Is blocked by by reversing that row. Run a transitive cycle check on the blocks graph inside the insert transaction. Store Relates to and Duplicates as separate rows. Reject a dependency from an issue to itself.

R-11 Project move. Keep project immutable on existing issues in v1, which matches the issue-key prefix rule. Editing project on the detail panel can wait until key migration exists.

R-12 Reminders. Store due dates as dates. Evaluate tomorrow, today, and overdue in one configured organization timezone, UTC until Settings defines it. Deduplicate on user, issue, and reminder type. If the due date changes, a new type-and-date pair may notify again. The worker inserts Notification rows only.

R-13 API. Use the JSON envelope for `/api/v1` routes. Leave Better Auth on its own routes. Paginate lists with `page`, `pageSize`, and `total`. Compare `updatedAt` on PATCH and return a conflict when it mismatches.

R-14 Search indexes. Index issue key, project, status, priority, assignee, due date, and updatedAt. Use a trigram index on title for search. Do not search description in v1.

R-15 Bootstrap. The migrate container creates the first admin from environment variables supplied at first boot, then the operator removes those values from the host environment. The image does not contain a default password.

title: Later Digitrac knowledge-base integration contract
questions: How should IssueFlow knowledge integrate with Digitrac later?
Can Digitrac AI reports answer IssueFlow questions?
May Digitrac automatically create an IssueFlow issue?
Which Mongo collections store this knowledge base?
text:
This record describes a later integration. It is not IssueFlow v1 scope. IssueFlow v1 non-goals exclude external integrations, automatic issue creation, and AI-generated issues.

Digitrac, in the repository `digitrail-onpremise`, is a separate on-prem product. It tracks inward documents, invoices, stock, and IQC in MongoDB. Relevant existing collections include `invoicedatas`, `invoicetranscations`, `stocks`, `iqcrecords`, and `llmtransactions`. Its current AI feature posts a query to FastAPI `/generate-report` with the tenant MongoDB URI and asks questions about that tenant's operational data. Token use is inserted into `llmtransactions` with a `typeOfLLM` string. That path is not a document knowledge base. It has no chunk store and no vector index.

Use this corpus for a second path that answers questions about the IssueFlow specification.

Proposed Digitrac collections, new and separate from invoices:

- `knowledgedocuments`: one row per source record, with `docId`, `corpus` = `issueflow`, `corpusVersion` = `issueflow-prd-1.0.0`, `kind`, `authority`, `title`, `prdSections`, `sourceFile`, and timestamps.
- `knowledgechunks`: the embeddable text, the embedding vector, `docId`, and the same filter fields. Load rows from `dist/issueflow-prd.jsonl` where `embed` is true.

Query rules:

- Retrieve only `corpus` = `issueflow` for IssueFlow questions.
- Do not send these chunks to `/generate-report` and do not query `invoicedatas` in the same retrieval.
- Log tokens with `typeOfLLM` = `issueflow-kb` so usage stays distinct from `aireports`.
- Cite `docId` and `prdSections` in the answer.
- When the best chunk has `authority` = `unspecified`, say the PRD does not decide it.
- When the best chunk has `authority` = `advisory`, call it a proposal.

Access: this corpus is product documentation for people building or operating IssueFlow. It is not plant invoice data. Gate it with a Digitrac permission for that audience. Do not inherit invoice ACLs, and do not expose it through the inward CSV folders.

A later product bridge from a Digitrac IQC or invoice screen to IssueFlow may prefill a draft. A person still submits the issue. Digitrac must not call IssueFlow to create, assign, or close an issue by itself. That would break the manual-first rule and the ban on automatic issue creation.

Live IssueFlow issues, if indexed later, are a different corpus, `issueflow-runtime`, filtered by that user's project permissions. Do not mix runtime issues into `issueflow-prd-1.0.0`.

title: Answer policy for a RAG system using this corpus
questions: How should a RAG answer behave when using the IssueFlow knowledge base?
What should the model do when the PRD does not specify something?
Which metadata filters should a retrieval query set?
text:
Use this policy when answering from the IssueFlow corpus.

Retrieve with metadata filters before vector similarity. For a product-behavior question, filter `corpus` = `issueflow` and `embed` = true. Prefer `kind` = `requirement` when the user asks what the product does. Include `kind` = `gap` when the user asks whether something is specified. Include `kind` = `recommendation` only when the user asks for a proposed default or an implementation choice. Include `kind` = `integration` when the user asks about Digitrac or RAG.

Answer only from retrieved records. Cite `docId` and `prdSections`. If records conflict, prefer `authority` = `normative` over `advisory` and `unspecified`.

If the retrieved gap record covers the question, say the PRD does not specify that behavior and name the gap id. Do not promote a recommendation into a requirement.

Do not describe automatic status changes, automatic assignment, automatic issue creation, email notifications, sprint metrics, time tracking, or GitHub, GitLab, Slack, or Jira sync as IssueFlow v1 features. Those are non-goals in `issueflow.prd.v1.boundaries`.

Embedding input for each record is the title, then the questions, then the text. Each record is one chunk. Do not merge chunks in the index. At answer time, pass the smallest set of chunks that covers the question so the manual-first rules stay in context for any behavior question.

The raw PRD file `source/IssueFlow_PRD.md` is provenance. It is not an embeddable chunk. Point a human at a PRD section from `prdSections` when they want the original wording.

title: Entity glossary for IssueFlow
questions: What are the main IssueFlow entities?
Is a subtask a separate entity?
What does ProjectMember represent?
text:
User: an account with an application role of Admin, Manager, or Member. Inactive users cannot log in. Their past activity remains.

Account, Session, Verification: Better Auth adapter records for credentials, sessions, and verification tokens.

Project: a named body of work with a unique key, optional description, active or archived status, creator, and creation time.

ProjectMember: the membership of a user on a project. This is the permit that limits which projects a Manager or Member can see and change.

Issue: the unit of work. It belongs to one project, has a generated key, a type, a status, a priority, an optional assignee, an automatic reporter, optional tags, an optional due date, an optional parent issue, and created and updated timestamps. A subtask is an Issue with a parent issue. It is not a separate entity.

Tag: a named, colored label that belongs to one project.

IssueTag: the many-to-many link between an issue and a tag.

Comment: Markdown text on an issue, with author and timestamp.

ActivityLog: a server-written history row for an issue change, stored in the same transaction as that change.

Attachment: metadata for a file stored on the `attachments` volume. The file bytes are not in PostgreSQL.

Dependency: a relationship between two issues. Types are Blocks, Is blocked by (the inverse view of Blocks), Relates to, and Duplicates.

Notification: an in-app notice for a user. It does not modify the issue.

SavedFilter: a stored combination of the supported issue filters.

Worker: a process, not a table. It reads due dates and writes reminder notifications. It does not change issue business fields.

title: Relationships between IssueFlow entities
questions: How are IssueFlow entities related?
What is the parent of a subtask?
What writes activity and notifications?
text:
Relationship statements that the PRD supports:

- A Project has many Issues. An Issue belongs to one Project.
- A Project has many Tags. A Tag belongs to one Project.
- An Issue has many Tags through IssueTag. A Tag can label many Issues in its project.
- A User joins a Project through ProjectMember.
- An Issue has one optional assignee User and one reporter User.
- An Issue has one optional parent Issue. That parent relationship is the subtask structure. The child has its own issue key.
- An Issue has many Comments, Attachments, ActivityLog rows, and Dependency rows.
- A Dependency connects two Issues and has a relationship type.
- A Notification is addressed to a User and refers to an issue event. Creating a notification does not update issue status, assignee, or priority.
- A SavedFilter belongs to the search feature. The PRD does not say it belongs to a user or a project.
- The application server writes ActivityLog in the same transaction as the issue update that caused it.
- The worker writes due-date Notification rows from dates stored on Issues.

Self-dependencies are forbidden. Circular blocking relationships are forbidden. The blocks relationship is directional: Is blocked by is the inverse representation of Blocks.
